upstream.sha_note: Not the v0.24.8 tag commit (ee35a6eb) but seven commits past it, which is the commit nvim-treesitter and Helix both pin. Six of the seven are CI/dependabot churn; the seventh, 46aa487b 'Include LICENSE file' (#49), adds "LICENSE" to Cargo.toml's include list. A redistribution has to ship its licence, so pinning the tag would have meant carrying that fix as a local patch — treebank-lua carries exactly that patch for exactly that omission. Cargo.toml's version at this sha still reads 0.24.8.

upstream_choice.summary: tree-sitter/tree-sitter-json is the grammar; there is no fork to choose between. The editors converge not merely on the repo but on the SAME COMMIT, 001c28d7a29832b06b0e831ec77845553c89b56d, which is the commit pinned here.
upstream_choice.evidence: nvim-treesitter (main) lua/nvim-treesitter/parsers.lua -> tree-sitter/tree-sitter-json @ 001c28d7, tier 2, maintainer @steelsojka; Helix languages.toml [[grammar]] name="json" -> same repo @ 001c28d7; Zed bundles JSON in the binary and depends on the crates.io crate tree-sitter-json = "0.24". 204 stars, last push 2025-11-24, 8 open issues, not archived. It sits in the tree-sitter/ org, which ROADMAP.md s3 measured as the only host with zero grammars over a year stale.
upstream_choice.alternatives_considered: None for JSON itself. The neighbouring dialects are separate decisions and route differently: JSON5 is a different language with its own grammar (Joakker/tree-sitter-json5, which Helix pins at 248b8564) and would be its own treebank crate; JSONC is NOT a separate grammar anywhere — Helix's `jsonc` language uses scope source.json and this same grammar, because tree-sitter-json already parses comments on purpose. So a future treebank JSONC is a `classify()` dialect hint plus a JSONC oracle, not a new submodule. Upstream issues #59 and #60 (both open) are about saying so in the README.

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger). Nothing in this grammar has an identifier rule, so the pin is inherited discipline rather than a measured need here — which is the point of pinning it everywhere.

oracle.tool: tools/json-oracle/check.mjs, run under node (stdin_oracle, one long-lived process)
oracle.dialect: RFC 8259 / ECMA-404 strict JSON, as implemented by V8's JSON.parse
oracle.note: V8's JSON.parse over the file's bytes. TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. This is the one language where 'parse-only, no project context' needed no arranging — JSON has no imports, no configuration and no execution, so there is nothing to disable and nothing to be missing. It is also the parser the corpus is actually consumed by: the corpus is npm packages, and what reads their .json files is V8.

positions.bom: A leading UTF-8 BOM makes a file INVALID. RFC 8259 s8.1 says implementations MAY ignore one, so this is a declared position rather than a fact. V8's JSON.parse rejects a BOM and this oracle is V8, not V8-plus-a-courtesy. It needs one line of vigilance to hold: TextDecoder('utf-8') STRIPS a BOM by default, so accepting one is what you get by accident; check.mjs passes ignoreBOM: true. Measured incidence in this corpus: 0 of 5,657 files, so the position costs nothing measurable either way and is recorded because it is invisible, not because it is expensive. The grammar accepts a BOM, so this position can only ever add noise, never a gap.
positions.utf8: JSON text MUST be UTF-8 (RFC 8259 s8.1), so an undecodable file is a REJECT and not an I/O error: the bytes were read fine, they are just not JSON text. fatal: true rather than letting U+FFFD replacement characters silently turn arbitrary bytes into a well-formed string. A UTF-16LE document is therefore invalid, which is in test/negative/.

oracle.self_test_note: check.mjs verifies V8's acceptance boundary on 15 embedded cases BEFORE it emits any verdict, and exits 3 if the engine disagrees, naming process.version. A recorded version string would only say which node is on PATH; this says whether that node's JSON.parse still draws the line these sweep numbers assume. The cases are the ones that separate strict JSON from the dialects it gets confused with (trailing comma, comment, single quotes, unquoted key, NaN, leading zero, short \u escape, empty document, two documents, BOM) plus the four where conformant parsers were measured to disagree (duplicate keys, lone surrogate, depth 200, top-level scalar). Cost: ~0.1 ms once per batch.
oracle.unreadable_note: An unreadable file is NOT an invalid file: anything that stops the oracle getting a file's bytes prints the path and reason to stderr and exits 2 without emitting a verdict. validate() only ever runs on files the grammar already failed and an 'invalid' verdict books the file as noise, so a mistyped corpus root that scored every file invalid would drive gap_files to zero and report a flawless grammar — which on a negative control is precisely the failure that would look like success.
oracle.stage_note: JSON.parse is the whole parser: there is no separate parse/compose/load split to choose between, because a JSON text IS its value. Recorded as a checked non-choice rather than left blank — the axis that cost yaml 73 files and python 11 does not exist here, and that is worth writing down.

populations.name: negative battery
populations.how_measured: 39 must-reject, 12 must-stay-valid, 3 declared positions, run through all three parsers

populations.name: real corpus
populations.how_measured: every .json in the fetched npm corpus
populations.blind_to: deep nesting and lone surrogates — measured zeros, so a zero here is not reassurance

considered.why_not: REJECTED as not conformant, and it was the obvious choice: already a CLI dependency, no subprocess, 3x faster. Two over-strict divergences. (1) It rejects nesting deeper than its default recursion limit — measured exactly at 127 valid / 128 invalid — where V8 and CPython accept depth 2000. (2) It rejects lone-surrogate escapes such as "\ud800", which RFC 8259 permits (it calls them not interoperable, not invalid). Over-strict is the dangerous direction: a valid file called invalid is booked as corpus noise, so the grammar failure that produced it disappears from gap_files silently. On the language whose whole job is to be a negative control, an oracle that quietly agrees with the grammar is the one defect the result cannot reveal.

considered.tool: CPython json.loads (parse_constant raising, so NaN/Infinity reject)
considered.cost: 0.07 s / 1000 files, batch, 0.03 s of it startup
considered.why_not: Would have worked. Not chosen for two reasons, neither damning: at ~100k nesting depth it raises RecursionError rather than ValueError, so it crashes the oracle instead of judging the file — loud, which is the acceptable failure, but V8's parser is iterative and has no depth limit at all; and the corpus is npm packages, whose .json files are read by V8 in practice, so V8 is the parser that decides whether these files work for their actual consumers. Default-lax on NaN/Infinity, which had to be turned off explicitly — a reminder that 'conformant' is a property of a call, not of a library.

smoke.note: The valid fixture is this ledger itself, and consumer-test's patched.json is deliberately NOT used: that fixture carries comments on purpose, because the grammar parses JSONC and the consumer test is about the grammar — so the strict oracle rightly calls it invalid. Lua's smoke block has the same shape of exception for the same reason. Pointing at this file instead is not a dodge: a ledger that stopped being strict JSON would be a real defect, and this is the cheapest place to catch it.

oracle_why_this_field_exists: generate_cli exists because regenerating with a different tree-sitter-cli silently changes what the grammar accepts. This exists because running a different reference parser silently changes what 'invalid' means. JSON is where you would least expect that to bite — one spec, one page of grammar, ROADMAP.md s5 says 'any conformant parser' — and it bites anyway: see oracle_not_serde_json. The cheapest, most obvious choice was measured to be the wrong one.

oracle_not_serde_json.summary: serde_json was the obvious oracle — the CLI already depends on it, it needs no subprocess, and it measured 0.02 s per 1000 files against V8's 0.08. It was REJECTED as not conformant. Three parsers all called conformant agree on 51 of 54 negative-battery cases and disagree on three, and the disagreements are all serde_json's, all in the over-strict direction.
oracle_not_serde_json.measured: Battery of 54 files (39 must-reject, 12 must-stay-valid, 3 open positions) against V8 22.23.2, CPython 3.12.3 json, and serde_json 1. All three: 51/51 correct on the settled cases. Divergences: (1) serde_json rejects nesting deeper than its default recursion limit — threshold measured exactly, 127 valid and 128 invalid — where V8 and CPython accept depth 2000; (2) serde_json rejects lone-surrogate escapes such as "\ud800", which RFC 8259 permits (it warns they are not interoperable, not that they are invalid); (3) CPython raises RecursionError, not ValueError, at ~100k depth, so it crashes the oracle rather than misjudging the file — loud, which is the acceptable failure. V8's parser is iterative and has no depth limit.
oracle_not_serde_json.why_it_matters: Over-strict is the DANGEROUS direction. A valid file called invalid is booked as corpus noise, so the grammar failure that produced it disappears from gap_files silently. Under-strict manufactures visible false gaps someone then investigates; over-strict manufactures a clean sweep. On the language whose whole job is to be a negative control, an oracle that quietly agrees with the grammar is the one defect that cannot be caught by the result.
oracle_not_serde_json.corpus_agreement_is_not_evidence: All three parsers agreed on 5,657 of 5,657 real corpus files and on 999 of 999 in the first sample. That agreement is worth nothing and is recorded only so it is not mistaken for evidence — the same conclusion treebank-php reached after its batch oracle matched php -l on all 1,703 files while accepting ten classes of invalid PHP. Only the battery separated them, and only on three cases.

oracle_cost.measured: 0.07-0.08 s per 1000 files, warm, single node process, absolute paths on stdin (the ROADMAP.md s9 protocol). Startup is 0.04 s of that, so the marginal cost is ~0.04 s / 1000. At scale it flattens further: the full 5,657-file corpus adjudicates in 0.485 s (0.086 s/1000 including startup), and 9,990 files in 0.32 s (0.032 s/1000).
oracle_cost.reject_path: No penalty, which is unusual. 999 files truncated to 60% — the input shape validate() actually sees — cost 0.09 s against 0.08 s for the same files whole. javascript pays 10.6x on this test because it falls through to a second parser; JSON has no second mode to fall into.
oracle_cost.roadmap_disagreement: ROADMAP.md s1 gives Tier A as 0.2-2 s per 1000 files, and s2's cheapest measured oracle is javascript at 0.21 s. JSON measures 0.08 s, 2.6x below the stated floor, so the band's bottom is wrong: it should read ~0.05-2 s. Reported because 90 more languages get costed against that table.
oracle_cost.sample: The headline number is 999 files (deterministic stride sample) from the top 800 npm packages: 3.1 MB, median 1.1 KB, p90 3.0 KB, max 438 KB. Startup-dominated at this size, so the figure tracks process startup more than it tracks bytes.

grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.summary: tree-sitter-json's language is a strict SUPERSET of RFC 8259 JSON, deliberately and upstream-documented. That relationship, not the corpus, is the structural reason this grammar cannot produce many gaps: a gap requires the grammar to be NARROWER than the oracle somewhere, and there was exactly one such place in the whole language (patch 0003).
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.evidence: Upstream's own test/corpus/main.txt carries a 'Comments' case whose comment reads 'we allow comments, because several commonly used tools allow comments in files with the extension `.json`', and a 'Multiple top-level objects' case. `comment` is in `extras` and `document` is `repeat($._value)`.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.measured_battery: Of the 54-case battery: 14 both accept, 29 both reject, 11 the grammar accepts and the oracle rejects, 0 the reverse. The 11: line comment, block comment, BOM, empty document, whitespace-only document, two top-level documents, JSONL, raw tab inside a string, a short \u12 escape, a trailing decimal point (1.), and invalid UTF-8 bytes inside a string.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.measured_corpus: Over all 5,657 corpus files: grammar rejects 92, oracle rejects 109, both reject 92, grammar-rejects-and-oracle-accepts (gaps) 0, grammar-accepts-and-oracle-rejects 17. The 17 are JSONC with comments but no trailing comma: 11 tsdoc-metadata.json, 5 tsconfig variants, one .vscode/launch.json.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.why_this_is_safe: The asymmetry runs grammar-accepts / oracle-rejects, which can never manufacture a gap; it only decides how much is booked as noise. gap_files stays exact.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.negative_corpus_consequence: test/negative/ may contain ONLY syntax that the grammar genuinely rejects, which rules out every one of the 11 classes above — no comments, no BOM, no empty or multi-document files, no raw tabs, no short \u escapes, no `1.`. Each of the 32 files there was verified rejected by BOTH the oracle and the patched grammar rather than assumed.

negative_control.summary: ROADMAP.md picks JSON as the negative control: 'The grammar should be perfect and the sweep should find nothing. A pipeline that reports gaps here is broken.' The measured result is not quite that. The pipeline is fine and the grammar was not perfect: the first sweep over a wide enough corpus found ONE real gap (patch 0003, the exponent's plus sign, which RFC 8259 explicitly allows and no upstream issue mentions). After it, 0 gaps.
negative_control.zero_is_verified_not_assumed: A zero from a pipeline that cannot report non-zero is worthless, so the pipeline was falsified rather than trusted. Mutation test: the same corpus and the same sweep against a grammar with `$.null` deleted from the `_value` choice reported 3 gap files (1426-file corpus), where the unmutated grammar reported 0. The path from 'grammar rejects a file' through 'oracle says valid' to 'gap_files > 0 and a cluster with a repro' therefore works end to end on this language.
negative_control.the_zero_is_structural: Zero gaps here is not luck and not corpus thinness — it follows from grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle. The grammar's language is a superset of the oracle's, so the only possible gaps are the places the grammar is narrower than RFC 8259, and JSON's grammar is small enough that those places can be enumerated: the number rule was the only one, and it was wrong.
negative_control.corpus_width_mattered_more_than_corpus_s: The first corpus (top 800 npm packages, 1,426 files) reported 0 gaps and would have been reported as a clean negative control. Widening to 3,000 packages (5,657 files) surfaced the exponent bug in ONE file. 76% of the first corpus was package.json — a single npm-authored schema that contains almost no numbers and no exponents at all. The lesson for the languages behind this one is that a guest language's corpus is a monoculture by default, and file COUNT is not the axis that fixes it.
negative_control.what_a_gap_here_would_have_meant: Had the gap been in the harness rather than the grammar, the tells were prepared for: an oracle that cannot fail loudly (exit 2 on unreadable, exit 3 on an engine whose JSON.parse moved), an oracle stricter than the spec (measured against two other parsers on a battery), and a corpus root that adjudicates to all-invalid. None fired. The one gap reproduced in three characters — `1e+1` — and reproduces against V8, CPython and serde_json alike.

corpus.source: npm registry tarballs for the top packages by download rank. JSON is a GUEST language: it owns no registry and no package, it only rides inside other people's, and npm is where it rides most — every published package carries at least one .json by construction.
corpus.ranking: npm-high-impact 1.13.0 (wooorm), the same list javascript and typescript use; lib/top.js's `top` array, in order.
corpus.files_note: .json only — the single extension tree-sitter-json's tree-sitter.json claims. .jsonc, .json5 and .geojson are deliberately not taken: json5 is a different language with a different grammar, and claiming an extension the grammar does not advertise is the silent widening python and lua refuse. Paths containing a node_modules component are excluded: a package that ships its own dependency tree is shipping other packages' files, and a failure there is attributed to the wrong package (the rule javascript applies to bundles and python to _vendor/). Measured: 294 of 5,951 files, 4.9%, from exactly two packages — npm (209) and pnpm (85). It was not cosmetic: before the exclusion the single gap file was counted twice, once as jsonparse's own fixture and once as npm's vendored copy of it.
corpus.monoculture: 3,665 of 5,657 files (65%) are named package.json, and 1,673 distinct basenames cover the rest. This is the corpus's central weakness and it is structural for a guest language: the file that appears in every package is the one npm itself specifies. package.json is almost entirely strings and objects, which is why it took a wider corpus rather than a bigger one to reach a number with an exponent in it. Recorded here because any future 'JSON sweeps clean' claim inherits this bias.
corpus.jsonc_note: 109 of 5,657 files (1.9%) are not strict JSON, and every single one is JSONC: trailing commas and/or comments, in tsconfig*.json (142 in the corpus), tsdoc-metadata.json, .vscode/*.json. They are kept rather than filtered because the grammar parses them on purpose — dropping them would flatter the noise column by hiding files this grammar handles. 92 fail the grammar (trailing commas, which it does not accept) and are booked as noise; 17 pass it (comments only). This is where a real JSONC dialect attaches later: a classify() dialect hint plus a JSONC oracle, no new grammar.

sweep_upstream.note: upstream 001c28d7 with the two packaging patches only, i.e. before patch 0003.

sweep_patched.note: with patch 0003. 98.37% of files parse; 100% of the strict JSON in the corpus parses, and every remaining failure is a JSONC trailing comma the oracle also rejects.

Cargo.lock carries the matching rename and nothing else. The published version string is deliberately NOT here: publish.sh derives it from crates.io at publish time. See PUBLISHING.md.
patches.note: Unlike lua, no LICENSE fix is needed: upstream added "LICENSE" to include in 46aa487b (Include LICENSE file, #49), which is one of the seven commits between tag v0.24.8 and the pinned sha and is part of why the pin is the commit the editors pin rather than the tag.

patches.title: exponent plus sign
patches.origin: treebank; found by this crate's first wide sweep. No upstream issue or PR covers it — all 63 issues were checked, the number-rule ones (#1 'Allow negative numbers', #18 'Number starts with a dot') are about the mantissa. Worth offering upstream as a one-token fix.

evidence.diagnosis: grammar.js's number rule defines `signedInteger = seq(optional('-'), decimalDigits)` and uses it for the exponent, so `e-1` and `e1` parse and `e+1` does not. RFC 8259 s6 is explicit — `exp = e [ minus / plus ] 1*DIGIT` — and ECMA-404 says the same, so this is a grammar bug rather than a dialect question; V8, CPython and serde_json all accept `1e+1`. The fix is `optional(choice('-', '+'))`, which touches nothing else: signedInteger is used ONLY by exponentPart, and the mantissa's sign comes from decimalIntegerLiteral's own `optional('-')`, so `+1` stays invalid.
evidence.evidence_note: One file in 5,657 and zero regressions, both measured over the identical corpus with only this patch removed and restored. The file is jsonparse's own sample document, which is a fair sample of what JSON-parser authors think is worth testing: it packs 0.5e+1, 2E+1, 0.8e-0 and 2E10 into one line. Beyond the sweep: upstream's corpus tests go 6/6 -> 7/7 with the exponent case added; the 32-file negative corpus is still fully rejected, including three cases added specifically to guard this widening (`1e+` with no digits, `1E++1`, `1e+.5`); and the consumer fixture patched.json parses Clean against the patched grammar and ERRORs at the `0.5e+1` column against the same tree with only this patch reverted.
